'''''Hyssopus officinalis''''' or '''hyssop''' is a [[shrub]] in the [[Lamiaceae]] or mint family native to Southern [[Europe]], the [[Middle East]], and the region surrounding the [[Caspian Sea]]. Due to its purported properties as an [[antiseptic]], [[cough|cough reliever]], and [[expectorant]], it has been used in [[traditional herbal medicine]].

==Description==
Hyssop is a brightly coloured shrub or [[subshrub]] that ranges from {{convert|30|to|60|cm|in|abbr=on}} in height. The [[plant stem|stem]] is [[lignin|woody]] at the base, from which grow a number of upright branches. Its [[leaf|leaves]] are [[leaf shape|lanceolate]], dark green, and from {{convert|2|to|2.5|cm|in|frac=8|abbr=on}} long.<ref>{{Cite book
| author = Pérez Maté, P.
| title = Especies aromáticas y medicinales
| year = 2002
| publisher = INTA
| location = Buenos Aires
| id = [http://www.inta.gov.ar/barrow/info/documentos/prohuerta/Arom%C3%A1ticas.pdf]
|language=es}}</ref>

During the summer, hyssop produces pink, blue (ssp. aristatus), or, more rarely, white [[fragrant]] (ssp. f. albus) [[flower]]s. These give rise to small oblong tetra-[[achene]]s.

==History==
{{main|Ezov}}

A plant called hyssop has been in use since [[classical antiquity]]. Its name is a direct adaptation from the [[Ancient Greek|Greek]] ὕσσωπος ({{transliteration|grc|hyssopos}}). The Hebrew word אזוב (''[[ezov]]'', ''esov'', or ''esob'') and the Greek word ὕσσωπος probably share a common (but unknown) origin.<ref>''Oxford English Dictionary'', 2nd Edition, 1989, ''s.v.'' hyssop</ref> The name hyssop appears as a translation of ''ezov'' in some translations of the Bible, notably in {{Bibleverse|Psalms|51:7|KJV}}: "Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean", but researchers have suggested that the Biblical accounts refer not to the plant currently known as hyssop but rather to one of a number of different herbs, including ''[[Origanum syriacum]]'' (Syrian oregano, commonly referred to as "bible hyssop").<ref>Based on the [[Judeo-Arabic]] translation of the word in the works of Rabbi [[Saadia Gaon]] (in his ''Tafsir'', a translation of the Pentateuch, Exodus 12:22), [[David ben Abraham al-Fasi]] (in his Hebrew–Arabic Dictionary of the Bible, known as ''`Kitāb Jāmiʿ al-Alfāẓ`'', vol. 1, s.v. אזוב), Rabbi [[Jonah ibn Janah]] (''Sefer HaShorashim'' – Book of the Roots, s.v. אזב – ''aleph'', ''zayn'', ''bet''), [[Maimonides]] (in his ''Mishnah'' Commentary, ''Nega'im'' 14:6) and [[Nathan ben Abraham I]] in Mishnah ''Uktzin'' 2:2. The problems with identification arise from Jewish oral tradition where it expressly prohibits Greek hyssop, and where the biblical plant is said to have been identical to the Arabic word, ''zaatar'' (''Origanum syriacum''), and which word is not to be associated with other ''ezobs'' that often bear an additional epithet, such as ''zaatar farsi'' = Persian-hyssop ([[Thymbra capitata]]) and ''zaatar rumi'' = Roman-hyssop ([[Satureja thymbra]]). See: ''[[The Mishnah]]'' (ed. [[Herbert Danby]]), Oxford University Press: Oxford 1977, s.v. ''Negai'im'' 14:6 ([https://archive.org/details/DanbyMishnah/page/n725 p. 696]); ''Parah'' 11:7 [10:7] ([https://archive.org/details/DanbyMishnah/page/n740 p. 711]).</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author1=Fleisher, A. |author2=Fleisher, Z. |year=1988 |title=Identification of biblical hyssop and origin of the traditional use of oregano-group herbs in the Mediterranean region |journal=Economic Botany |volume=42 |issue=2 |pages=232–241 |doi=10.1007/bf02858924|bibcode=1988EcBot..42..232F |s2cid=45220405 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=The Biblical Problem of Hyssop |url=http://www.biblicalstudies.org.uk/pdf/eq/hyssop_harrison.pdf |journal=The Evangelical Quarterly |volume=26 |issue=4 |year=1954 |pages=218–224 |author=R. K. Harrison |doi=10.1163/27725472-02604004 |s2cid=256487464 |access-date=2012-11-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160331201420/http://biblicalstudies.org.uk/pdf/eq/hyssop_harrison.pdf |archive-date=2016-03-31 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Origanum+syriacum|title=Origanum syriacum Bible Hyssop PFAF Plant Database|website=pfaf.org}}</ref> {{Bibleverse|1 Kings|4:33|KJV}} mentions that 'ezov' was a small plant and some scholars believe it was a wall plant.<ref name=balfour>{{cite book |last1=Balfour |first1=John Hutton |title=The plants of the Bible, trees and shrubs |year=1866 |page=[https://archive.org/details/plantsbibletree01balfgoog/page/n48 34] |url=https://archive.org/details/plantsbibletree01balfgoog |access-date=27 August 2019}}</ref> It was burned with the [[red heifer]] ({{Bibleverse|Numbers|19:6|KJV}}) and used for purification of lepers ({{Bibleverse|Leviticus|14:4-6|KJV}}, {{Bibleverse|Leviticus|14:49-51|KJV}}; {{Bibleverse|Numbers|19:18|KJV}}), and at [[Passover]] it was used to sprinkle the blood of the [[sacrificial lamb]] on the doorposts ({{Bibleverse|Exodus|12:22|KJV}}).<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.jewishencyclopedia.com/articles/7974-hyssop|title=HYSSOP - JewishEncyclopedia.com|website=www.jewishencyclopedia.com|access-date=2016-05-28}}</ref> A sponge attached to a hyssop branch was used to give [[Jesus]] on the [[Crucifixion of Jesus|cross]] a drink of vinegar.<ref>{{Bibleverse|John|19:29|KJV}}</ref>

Suggestions abound for the modern day correlation of biblical hyssop ranging from a wall plant like moss or fern, to widely used culinary herbs like [[thyme]], [[rosemary]] or [[marjoram]]. Another suggestion is the [[caper]] plant which is known to grow in the rocky soils of the region and along walls.<ref name=balfour />

Hyssop was also used for [[Ritual purification|purgation]] (religious purification) in Egypt, where, according to [[Chaeremon of Alexandria|Chaeremon the Stoic]], the priests used to eat it with bread in order to purify this type of food and make it suitable for their austere diet.<ref>From Chaeremon's ''History of Egypt'', as quoted by [[Porphyry (philosopher)|Porphyry]], ''[[On Abstinence from Eating Animals|De Abstinentia]]'' [http://www.ccel.org/ccel/pearse/morefathers/files/porphyry_abstinence_04_book4.htm IV.6.9].</ref>

==Essential oil==
The [[essential oil]] includes the chemicals [[thujone]] and [[phenol]], which give it antiseptic properties.<ref>{{Cite book
  | last1 = van Wyk
  | first1 = Ben-Erik
  | last2 = Wink
  | first2 = Michael
  | title = Medicinal Plants of the World
  | publisher = Timber Press, Incorporated
  | year = 2004
  | edition = 1
  | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=bTdoTayyVrEC&q=hyssop+herb+expectorant&pg=PA177
  | isbn = 978-0-88192-602-6
  }}, p 177.</ref> Its high concentrations of thujone and chemicals that stimulate the [[central nervous system]], including [[pinocamphone]] and [[cineole]], can provoke [[epilepsy|epileptic]] reactions.<ref>{{cite journal | journal = J Neurol | date = 1999 | volume = 246 | issue = 8 | pages = 667–670 |author1=Pierre R. Burkhard |author2=Karim Burkhardt |author3=Charles-Antoine Haenggeli |author4=Theodor Landis | title = Plant-induced seizures: reappearance of an old problem | pmid= 10460442| doi = 10.1007/s004150050429 | s2cid = 20996610 }}</ref> The oil of hyssop can cause seizures and even low doses (2–3 drops) can cause convulsions in children.<ref>[http://www.webmd.com/vitamins-supplements/ingredientmono-258-HYSSOP.aspx?activeIngredientId=258&activeIngredientName=HYSSOP Hyssop], WebMD</ref>

==Herbal medicine==
In [[herbal medicine]] hyssop is believed to have soothing, expectorant, and [[cough suppressant]] properties.<ref>{{cite web
  | last = Grieve
  | first = M.
  | title = Hyssop: A Modern Herbal
  | publisher = Botanical.com
  | url = http://www.botanical.com/botanical/mgmh/h/hyssop48.html}}</ref> Hyssop has been used for centuries in [[traditional medicine]] in order to increase circulation and to treat multiple conditions such as coughing and sore throats.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://livertox.nih.gov/Hyssop.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130218110728/http://www.livertox.nih.gov/Hyssop.htm |url-status=dead |archive-date=February 18, 2013 |title=Hyssop |website=livertox.nih.gov}}</ref> Hyssop can stimulate the [[Gastrointestinal tract|gastrointestinal]] system.<ref>{{Cite book
  | last1 = Crellin
  | first1 = John
  | last2 = Philpott
  | first2 = Jane
  | title = A Reference Guide to Medicinal Plants: Herbal Medicine Past and Present
  | publisher = Duke University Press
  | year = 1997
  | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=0JaqB07uTx4C&q=hyssop+herbal+medicine&pg=PA257
  | isbn = 978-0-8223-1019-8
  }}
</ref>
